body.text: For India, Karakoram-2026 must be assessed against the interconnected challenges posed by China along the LAC and Pakistan along the LOC and the international border

The China-Pakistan defence partnership has long rested on strategic convergence, defence-industrial cooperation, and shared regional security concerns. The Karakoram-2026 joint military exercise marks a further evolution in this relationship by extending bilateral military engagement to regular army formations. Conducted from October 14 to 22 at a training facility near Korla in China’s Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, it was the first joint training exercise involving regular units of the People’s Liberation Army and the Pakistan Army. Its significance lies not merely in the activities undertaken but in the gradual shift towards greater operational familiarity between the two militaries.

Officially framed as a counter-terrorism exercise in high-altitude terrain, Karakoram-2026 involved unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations, target acquisition and firing on the move, long-range sniping, joint command procedures, mixed formations, task-based grouping and coordinated live-force manoeuvres. China supplied virtually all the equipment used, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armoured assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, unmanned platforms and counter-UAV systems.

Together, these activities indicate an effort to deepen tactical cooperation, improve familiarity with equipment and develop common operating procedures. Although the exercise does not establish an integrated China-Pakistan military capability, it signals a more operationally grounded defence relationship.

Three developments, in particular, stand out. First, the participation of regular army formations represents an expansion of bilateral military engagement. Earlier exercises, including the Warrior series, primarily involved special forces and specialised units engaged in counter-terrorism. Karakoram-2026 extends cooperation to regular land forces, creating opportunities to practise joint command, coordinated manoeuvres and mixed-unit operations. This transition matters because regular-force training potentially has wider implications for conventional military preparedness than exercises confined to specialised units.

Second, the exercise broadens the institutional framework of defence cooperation. The Warrior series focuses on specialised and counter-terrorism operations, Shaheen covers air forces, and Sea Guardian addresses maritime cooperation. Karakoram-2026 adds a dedicated land-forces dimension. These initiatives do not demonstrate the existence of an integrated tri-service command but their cumulative effect is to expand military engagement across operational domains.

Third, the exercise combines operational learning with technological familiarisation. Pakistani personnel gain exposure to Chinese platforms and systems that already feature prominently in Pakistan’s defence inventory. This could facilitate future procurement, training and equipment integration. China, too, gains opportunities to evaluate equipment and procedures in challenging mountainous terrain while drawing on Pakistan’s experience in counter-insurgency operations.

The partnership also has a practical security dimension. Both countries have interests in countering militant threats affecting Chinese personnel and CPEC infrastructure, particularly in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region. Training in surveillance, drone operations, counter-drone measures and high-altitude responses provides a mechanism for strengthening cooperation in these areas. The broader significance is that political trust and defence-industrial ties are increasingly being supplemented by opportunities to develop common operational practices. The extent to which this translates into effective coordination during an actual military contingency, however, remains uncertain.

For India, Karakoram-2026 must be assessed against the interconnected challenges posed by China along the Line of Actual Control and Pakistan along the Line of Control and the international border. Although officially designated a counter-terrorism exercise, its implications extend beyond that narrow description because several of the capabilities practised have potential applications in conventional operations.

For India, the concern is not that Karakoram-2026 has created a ready-made joint war-fighting capability. Rather, repeated exercises could gradually reduce the practical barriers to military coordination between two countries whose strategic interests already overlap.

Geography adds to its strategic significance. Korla is situated in Xinjiang, a region central to China’s western military posture, including contingencies concerning the Indian frontier. The broader area’s proximity to the Karakoram region reinforces its geopolitical relevance. The disputed Shaksgam Valley is particularly significant: Pakistan transferred control of the territory to China under the 1963 boundary agreement, which India rejects. Its significance emerges from the combination of geography, the capabilities practiced, and the wider trajectory of China-Pakistan military engagement.

Interoperability is the principal concern. Joint command procedures, mixed formations, UAV integration and familiarity with common equipment can improve coordination and reduce operational friction. High-altitude mobility, precision engagement and the management of forces in difficult terrain also have relevance beyond counter-terrorism. For India, the concern is not that Karakoram-2026 has created a ready-made joint war-fighting capability. Rather, repeated exercises could gradually reduce the practical barriers to military coordination between two countries whose strategic interests already overlap. This becomes particularly relevant when India must prepare for contingencies involving pressure on its northern and western fronts, either simultaneously or in succession.

India’s response should focus on improving operational resilience. First, New Delhi must strengthen all-weather logistics, surveillance and high-altitude mobility across its northern and western theatres. The ability to move and sustain forces in difficult geographical and climatic conditions remains essential to managing contingencies across multiple fronts.

Second, counter-UAV capabilities, layered air defence and electronic warfare will become increasingly important as unmanned systems are integrated into reconnaissance, targeting and battlefield operations. The emphasis on drones and counter-drone measures in Karakoram-2026 reinforces the need for a networked approach to situational awareness and force protection.

Third, India must continue improving joint planning, command arrangements and inter-service coordination. The challenge posed by closer China-Pakistan military cooperation concerns not only the forces either country can deploy but also the speed with which India can identify threats, allocate resources and respond across different theatres.

The larger strategic lesson for India is that the China-Pakistan relationship must be assessed not simply through arms transfers or diplomatic declarations but through the gradual development of shared operational experience, common procedures and technological compatibility.

Finally, India needs sustained intelligence collection and careful monitoring of changes in Chinese and Pakistani doctrine, equipment and force posture. Strategic preparedness requires distinguishing demonstrated capabilities from potential future scenarios, avoiding both complacency and overreaction.

The larger strategic lesson for India is that the China-Pakistan relationship must be assessed not simply through arms transfers or diplomatic declarations but through the gradual development of shared operational experience, common procedures and technological compatibility. India’s response must combine credible two-front preparedness, stronger joint war-fighting capabilities, and a clear-eyed assessment of the evolving regional balance.
This commentary originally appeared in The Telegraph.
